profile.name: Danza de la Botella
profile.tagline: Paraguayan folk dance balancing glass bottles on the head.
profile.insight: Advanced dancers balance ten or more glass bottles stacked on their heads while dancing Paraguayan polka.
profile.profile: Danza de la Botella is a Paraguayan folk dance where female dancers balance glass bottles on their heads while performing improvised moves to Paraguayan polka music. Originating possibly from the galopa dance, it features 19th-century rural costumes and emphasizes balance and grace. Dancers hold their skirts' ruffles with outstretched arms to maintain poise, performing solo or in groups. Bottles are decorated with ribbons or flowers and specially designed to stack securely without attaching to the head.
profile.profile_long: Danza de la Botella is a traditional folk dance from Paraguay distinguished by performers balancing glass bottles on their heads. Female dancers typically wear ankle-length skirts reminiscent of 19th-century rural Paraguayan attire. The dance likely evolved from the galopa folk dance, which involved balancing jugs on the head, with bottles replacing jugs over time. Performances are accompanied by Paraguayan polka music, a lively genre that sets the rhythm and mood. The dance is largely improvised, with basic movements involving dancers extending their arms to hold the ruffles of their skirts, creating an illusion that no bottles are balanced atop their heads. The dance can be performed individually, in pairs, or groups, with each dancer balancing one or two bottles. More skilled dancers can balance ten or more bottles stacked. The bottles are often decorated with tricolored ribbons reflecting the Paraguayan flag or adorned with flowers. When multiple bottles are stacked, they are designed to attach to each other securely but not to the dancer’s head, ensuring safety and balance. The dance has appeared in popular culture, including tasks on The Amazing Race and performances on Got Talent España, highlighting its cultural significance and visual appeal. The dance’s improvisational nature and the technical skill required to balance multiple bottles while moving to polka music make it a striking and challenging folk tradition.

sections.origins_and_history: The origin of Danza de la Botella remains unclear, but one theory suggests it derived from the galopa folk dance, which involved dancers balancing jugs on their heads. Over time, glass bottles replaced the jugs, evolving into the current form of the dance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Female dancers wear ankle-length skirts and balance glass bottles on their heads while dancing to Paraguayan polka music. Movements are mostly improvised, with dancers holding the ruffles of their skirts with outstretched arms to maintain balance and the illusion of no bottles. The dance can be performed solo, in pairs, or groups. Beginners start with balancing one or two bottles; advanced dancers can balance ten or more stacked bottles. Bottles used for stacking are designed to attach to each other but not to the head.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by Paraguayan polka music, a lively folk genre. Specific instruments or tempo details are not described in the sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear 19th-century rural Paraguayan costumes, including ankle-length skirts. Bottles are decorated with tricolored ribbons resembling the Paraguayan flag or with flowers. Performances occur in various settings, including cultural festivals and popular media events.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is a folk tradition performed in cultural celebrations and has gained visibility through popular media such as The Amazing Race and Got Talent España. It showcases balance, grace, and Paraguayan cultural identity.
sections.notable_figures: Notable performers include Belén Torres and Erika Vega, who performed the dance on Got Talent España, balancing five and ten bottles respectively.
sections.regional_variants: No regional variants are described in the sources.
sections.lineage: Danza de la Botella is linked to the galopa folk dance, sharing the concept of balancing vessels on the head, evolving from jugs to glass bottles.

claims.text: La danza de la botella es una danza folclórica tradicional de Paraguay en la que los artistas bailan con botellas de vidrio en equilibrio sobre sus cabezas.
claims.quote: La danza de la botella es una danza folclórica tradicional de Paraguay en la que los artistas bailan con botellas de vidrio en equilibrio sobre sus cabezas.

claims.text: El origen de la danza de la botella sigue sin estar claro. Una teoría es que la danza se derivó de la danza folclórica galopa, que consiste en bailarines que actúan con jarras sobre la cabeza, y los bailarines reemplazan las jarras con botellas de vidrio.
